answer_sql:
WITH per_product AS (
  SELECT
    p.product_key,
    p.product_name,
    COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN st.country_code <> '--' THEN st.country_code END) AS n_store,
    MIN(CASE WHEN st.country_code <> '--' THEN st.country_code END) AS store_cc,
    COUNT(DISTINCT c.country_code) AS n_cust,
    MIN(c.country_code) AS cust_cc,
    SUM(CASE WHEN s.channel = 'online' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS online_lines
  FROM contoso_served.v_contoso5_sales_line AS s
  JOIN contoso_served.dim_store AS st
    ON s.store_key = st.store_key
  JOIN contoso_served.dim_customer AS c
    ON s.customer_key = c.customer_key
  JOIN contoso_served.dim_product AS p
    ON s.product_key = p.product_key
  GROUP BY
    p.product_key,
    p.product_name
)
SELECT
  'a: selling shop country' AS reading,
  p.product_name AS product,
  dc.country_name AS country,
  p.n_store AS countries_sold_in
FROM per_product AS p
JOIN contoso_served.dim_country AS dc
  ON p.store_cc = dc.country_code
WHERE
  p.n_store = 1
UNION ALL
SELECT
  'b: buyer country',
  p.product_name,
  dc.country_name,
  p.n_cust
FROM per_product AS p
JOIN contoso_served.dim_country AS dc
  ON p.cust_cc = dc.country_code
WHERE
  p.n_cust = 1
UNION ALL
SELECT
  'c: selling shop country, strict',
  p.product_name,
  dc.country_name,
  p.n_store
FROM per_product AS p
JOIN contoso_served.dim_country AS dc
  ON p.store_cc = dc.country_code
WHERE
  p.n_store = 1 AND p.online_lines = 0
ORDER BY
  reading,
  country,
  product

sections.title: What it says its rows are

body.value: What I have calculated: for each of the 2,517 products Contoso has ever sold, in how many distinct countries that product's sales landed — counted once for each way this data can say where a sale happened — over all ten years of orders with both channels included and no date limit; then the products whose count is exactly one, each beside the single country it was sold in. The claimed answer is not one table but the choice between three, because the count of countries per product depends on which country column is read: 20 product-and-country rows by the selling shop's country, the identical 20 by the shop's site country, 4 rows by the buyer's country, and 1 row by the selling shop's country when a web sale is held to be a sale somewhere else. The figure in each row, "how many countries it was sold in", is 1 by construction — it is the test that selected the row, not an independent measurement, and that is the one column in the requested output that carries no information. What I did NOT include: no period restriction, no channel restriction, no product rollup, and no money or units figure of any kind — the only quantity here is a count of distinct countries per product.

value:
When you say a product was "sold in one country", do you mean the country of the shop that sold it, or the country the buyer lives in? Point at one and I will hand you that table:

(a) THE COUNTRY OF THE SELLING SHOP — a 20-row table. 17 products sold only in the United States (among them Adventure Works Floor Lamp M2150 Grey, Adventure Works Wall Lamp E2150 Grey, Litware Desk Lamp E1020 Black, Litware Floor Lamp M2015 Black, Litware Floor Lamp X1015 Blue), plus exactly one product each in three other countries: Adventure Works Chandelier M6150 Grey in Canada, Litware Floor Lamp M2015 White in the Netherlands, and Adventure Works Desk Lamp E1300 Black in the United Kingdom. Reading this as the shop's SITE country instead gives the identical 20 products with zero disagreements, so that is not a third answer.

(b) THE COUNTRY THE BUYER LIVES IN — a 4-row table, all four United States.

(c) THE COUNTRY OF THE SELLING SHOP, STRICTLY — only products whose every sale was rung up in that one country, so any product that also sold through the web shop is out: a 1-row table, United States. This reading exists because the web shop has no country of its own, and 19 of the 20 products in (a) also sold through it — they qualify in (a) only because the web shop's country code is a placeholder rather than a place.

WHAT THE CHOICE COSTS, CONCRETELY: going from (a) to (b) drops 16 of the 20 products, and those 16 include every non-US row — so (a) is the only reading under which Canada, the Netherlands and the United Kingdom appear at all. If you want a list that can name a country other than the United States, you want (a).

WHAT THE CHOICE DOES NOT CHANGE: at least 2,497 of the 2,517 products sold are ruled out as multi-country under every reading, and the United States dominates all three lists (17 of 20, 4 of 4, 1 of 1). The 4 products in (b) all sit inside the 20 in (a), so the readings never call the same product single-country and multi-country in opposite directions — the looser reading simply admits 16 more. Every single-country product is a lamp or chandelier under all three readings. Nothing is excluded for never having been sold: all 2,517 products on the register have sales, and no product sells only online. No date limit is in play — you named no period, so all ten years of orders are covered, 2016-05-18 to 2025-12-31.

All 2,517 products on dim_product, which measured is every product with at least one sales line — so the "never sold are left out" exclusion removed nothing. Computed over all 223,974 rows of v_contoso5_sales_line inner-joined to dim_store, dim_customer and dim_product (and dim_location for the third path); every join is declared cardinality 1 and the product total stayed 2,517 across all five queries, so no lines were dropped. NO date filter, per order.default.an_unscoped_question_covers_all_time (confidence C) and no period in the question: full extent of order_date, 2016-05-18 to 2025-12-31, on order_date and not delivery_date per order.default.period_is_order_date. NO channel filter: web-shop lines are in the population, because store.resolution.the_channel_is_the_location_sentinel scopes its `physical` default with `applies: subject` and this question's subject is a Product, not a Store. On the shop and site paths the `--` code is excluded from the COUNTRY COUNT per country.exclusion.sentinel_is_not_a_country — the online lines remain in the population, they merely contribute no country, which is exactly what separates reading (a) from reading (c). The country universe is the 8 real countries on every path. I did NOT restrict by channel, period, category, brand, price or revenue, and I did NOT roll products up into lines or categories.

)

  product_name,

The claimed answer is not one table but the choice between three, because the count of countries per product depends on which country column is read: 20 product-and-country rows by the selling shop's country, the identical 20 by the shop's site country, 4 rows by the buyer's country, and 1 row by the selling shop's country when a web sale is held to be a sale somewhere else. The figure in each row, "how many countries it was sold in", is 1 by construction — it is the test that selected the row, not an independent measurement, and that is the one column in the requested output that carries no information. One row stands for one product and its only country; products sold in two or more countries, and products never sold at all, are left out. No date limit is applied — all sales on record count.
